 The Government Is Mailing $500 Checks to Nearly 1 Million Americans (Are You Getting One?)
 Adam Palasciano 2026년 10월 19일 월 오전 9:30 UTC 0 
A surprise $500 check from the federal government is already heading to hundreds
of thousands of Americans. The Treasury Department began mailing payments on Sept.
30 to more than 950,000 people, according to CNBC. For households trying to get ahead financially ,
an unexpected $500 could certainly help.
But this isn't a new stimulus payment available to everyone. The checks are tied
specifically to Affordable Care Act (ACA) Marketplace coverage, and the
eligibility rules exclude the vast majority of Americans. The key is
understanding exactly which coverage and payment history count.
Here's what you need to know.
 Find Out: 14 moves seniors could benefit from but often forget about. 
 You need qualifying HealthCare.gov coverage
The White House says the $500 payments are going to people who bought
Marketplace insurance without receiving premium assistance, meaning they paid
the full premium rather than having a premium tax credit lower the cost. The
payments are $500 per eligible person, not per household, so a family with
multiple qualifying enrollees could receive more than one check.
Most recipients are expected to be people with incomes above 400% of the federal
poverty level — roughly $63,000 for one person or $129,000 for a family of four
— who lost federal premium assistance when the enhanced ACA subsidies expired.
Some people with incomes between 100% and 400% of the poverty level may also
qualify. The Trump administration says the payments are coming from surplus
Marketplace user-fee revenue that it argues was ultimately passed on to
consumers through higher premiums.
There is no separate application to submit — eligible recipients have already
been identified from Marketplace records.

 Only people in these 30 states are included
The program applies to people whose 2026 Marketplace coverage used the federal
HealthCare.gov platform.
CMS lists the 30 states as Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, Delaware,
Florida, Hawaii, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi,
Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, New Hampshire, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio,
Oklahoma, Oregon, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, West
Virginia, Wisconsin, and Wyoming.
 Advertisement
 The reason for the checks is disputed
The Trump administration describes the payments as refunds of excessive
Marketplace "user fees." The White House says insurers passed those fees through
to consumers in premiums, while the federal government collected more than it
needed to operate HealthCare.gov and accumulated an unused surplus.
There is another interpretation, however. CMS's 2026 payment rule, finalized in
January 2025, set the federal Marketplace user fee at 2.5% of monthly premiums
specifically to fund exchange operations based partly on expected enrollment. As
reported by the Associated Press, a KFF analysis indicated that some $1 billion
in unspent funds may trace back to user fees collected during Trump's first
administration, complicating the claim that the entire surplus resulted from
Biden-era overcharges.
 Grow Your $$: 9 things you must try when your savings reach $50,000 
 You don't need to apply or pay anyone
If you qualify, there's no form to fill out and no processing fee to pay. The
payments are being mailed automatically, and reporting on the program says
recipients don't need to take additional action to receive them.
That makes the program an obvious target for scammers. The Federal Trade
Commission warns that legitimate government agencies don't require you to pay
money or hand over financial-account information to receive a refund. Be
especially suspicious of texts, emails, or calls asking you to provide banking
information to "unlock" a $500 payment.
 This isn't a Medicare or tariff-dividend check
For people approaching retirement, the distinction matters. This $500 payment is
connected to ACA Marketplace insurance, which many people use before becoming
eligible for Medicare at 65. Medicare isn't part of the ACA Marketplace, and
people who already have Medicare likely don't use Marketplace coverage.
The payment is also separate from proposals for a much larger tariff-funded
"dividend." Those proposals have been discussed publicly but are not the same
program as these ACA refunds. Likewise, the $500 Marketplace payment isn't a
general IRS stimulus or direct-deposit program available simply because you
filed a tax return.
 Bottom line
Were you enrolled through HealthCare.gov in 2026, paid your Marketplace premium
without a tax credit, and lived in one of the 30 participating states? If so,
you may be among the more than 950,000 people receiving a $500 Treasury check
automatically. If you received premium assistance, used a separate state
Marketplace, or were already covered through Medicare instead, this particular
refund generally isn't aimed at you.
If you're uncertain, verify your Marketplace history through your HealthCare.gov
account or contact the official Marketplace Call Center at 1-800-318-2596 rather
than responding to an unsolicited message. A legitimate $500 payment won't solve
every affordability problem, but putting unexpected money toward essentials,
debt, or savings could help you cope with increasing
bills without putting your personal information at risk.
